title: Nicodemus by night (John 3:1–8)
hook: born again of water and the Spirit; the Church hears baptism here
carry: the wind bloweth where it will

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first sign at Cana: water into wine. Your line was the good wine until now. Did you save something good for late in the day? Day four hundred ninety-seven.

Some questions only come out at night. At two in the morning, lying awake, you finally ask what you couldn't ask at lunch. Today a man comes to Jesus with exactly that kind of question, and John tells us he came by night. His name is Nicodemus. He's a Pharisee, a respected teacher, a ruler among his people, a serious student of the scriptures. He has seen the signs and he's honest about it. Rabbi, he says, we know you are a teacher come from God. Nobody could do these signs unless God were with him. And Jesus answers a question he hasn't asked yet.
screen: `QUESTIONS THAT COME AT NIGHT.` → `A RESPECTED TEACHER.` → `RABBI, WE KNOW.`

segments.voice: Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Amen, amen I say to thee, unless a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God." The Greek word translated again, anothen, can also mean from above. Born again, born from above. John seems to want both. Nicodemus takes it literally, and asks the obvious, almost comic question: can a grown man go back into his mother's womb? Jesus goes further: "unless a man be born again of water and the Holy Ghost, he cannot enter into the kingdom of God." Water and the Spirit. This is where the Catholic Church hears baptism. The Catechism calls baptism a new birth by water and the Spirit and points to this very verse. Since the earliest centuries, Christians coming up out of the font have been called newly born. Then Jesus reaches for a picture. In Greek, the word pneuma means both wind and spirit, the same word. So the line can be read two ways. The Douay-Rheims, following the Latin, reads it as Spirit: "The Spirit breatheth where he will; and thou hearest his voice, but thou knowest not whence he cometh, and whither he goeth." Many other English Bibles, the King James among them, read it as wind, blowing wherever it will. Today's line holds that second reading. Both are faithful to the Greek, and the point is the same. You can't see the wind. You can't steer it. You hear it in the trees and you see what it moves. Nicodemus, the careful scholar, is being told that this new birth is not something he can schedule. And he doesn't vanish from the story. John will bring him back twice, the last time carrying a hundred pounds of spices to the tomb.
screen: `BORN AGAIN, BORN FROM ABOVE.` · `WATER AND THE HOLY GHOST.` · `PNEUMA: WIND AND SPIRIT.` · `NICODEMUS WILL BE BACK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask your question at night. Settle, and breathe. Let a question come that you usually keep for the dark. About God, about yourself, about someone you love, about what happens after. The question you'd only ask at two in the morning. Don't answer it. Just let it be asked, out loud in your head, the way Nicodemus asked his. Notice that you're allowed to ask it. If you pray, you can bring it to God as it is. If you don't, just hold it honestly. The bell holds the time.
Anothen. The Greek word meaning both again and from above, at the heart of Jesus' answer to Nicodemus in the dark. Today's word.

Your line: the wind bloweth where it will. Today, feel the wind, or a fan, and remember what you can't control. And that's week seventy-one: great joy, logos, the Word made flesh, Agnus Dei, the fig tree, the first sign, and Nicodemus. Day four hundred ninety-seven.
screen: `WEEK SEVENTY-ONE: JOY · LOGOS · FLESH · AGNUS DEI · FIG TREE · SIGN · NICODEMUS`

howItsDone: The Catholic Church reads John 3:5 as speaking of baptism, the new birth by water and the Spirit, and this passage is often read at baptisms and in the Easter season.

pairs: a Pharisee who came by night

myth: he came honestly: rabbi, we know you are a teacher come from God.

pneuma. the Douay reads Spirit, the King James reads wind.
he returns twice in John, the last time bringing spices for Jesus's burial.

fork.setup: you're Nicodemus. this teacher has just told you a man must be born again. you're a grown man and a scholar. what do you ask?
options: how can a man be born when he is old?
fork.reveal: he takes it literally and asks how a man can enter his mother's womb again. Jesus answers: of water and the Spirit.

original.note: Greek: again, anew, and also from above (John 3:3). Both senses seem meant.

trapdoor: what you thought: born again is a phrase about a personal conversion moment.
what it means: in Catholic teaching, born of water and the Spirit is baptism, the new birth into God's life.
what a scholar hears: anothen means both again and from above, and pneuma means both wind and spirit; John plays on both.

The carry 'the wind bloweth where it will' blends the KJV ('where it listeth') with modern wording; the Douay reads 'The Spirit breatheth where he will'. The script explains both readings without ranking. Confirm.
CCC 1215 and 1257 cite John 3:5 for baptism as new birth; paraphrased. Confirm.
'A hundred pounds' of myrrh and aloes (John 19:39, Roman pounds, about 75 modern pounds). Confirm phrasing.
Nicodemus is presented respectfully as a Pharisee and teacher; confirm the framing avoids using Pharisees as a foil.

Audit (10% sample): the KJV wording of John 3:8 was cited as a quotation; the Catholic path quotes the Douay, so the wind reading is now paraphrased and the KJV source entry removed. The index carry keeps its wording.
